title: Advanced Scheduling and Capacity
subtitle: Scheduler internals, placement rules, spreading, priorities and autoscaling
description: Understand exactly how Kubernetes places pods and plan the capacity behind them: scheduler phases, QoS, affinity, taints, topology spread, priorities, PDBs and autoscaling.
outcomes: Explain why a pod is Pending and which rule blocked it
Design placement with affinity, taints and topology spread for zone-level HA
Combine priorities, PDBs and autoscalers into a safe capacity strategy

modules.title: How placement works
modules.summary: Scheduler decisions, resource accounting and placement rules.

lessons.title: How the scheduler decides
lessons.summary: Filter and score phases, requests versus limits, QoS classes and node-pressure eviction.
objectives: Describe the scheduler filter and score phases
Explain why scheduling uses requests, not limits or live usage
Predict the QoS class of a pod and its eviction order

sections.title: Filter, then score, then bind
sections.body:
For every unscheduled pod, `kube-scheduler` runs a **scheduling cycle**. In the **filter** phase (predicates) it removes every node that cannot run the pod: not enough allocatable CPU or memory, untolerated taints, a failing `nodeSelector` or affinity rule, a missing volume zone, or a port conflict. If no node survives, the pod stays `Pending` with a `FailedScheduling` event.

In the **score** phase the surviving nodes get 0-100 points from plugins such as `NodeResourcesFit` (spread or bin-pack), `ImageLocality`, `InterPodAffinity` and `PodTopologySpread`. The highest score wins, ties are broken randomly, and the **bind** step writes `spec.nodeName`. The kubelet on that node then starts the containers.

sections.title: About this example: a pod that cannot be scheduled
sections.body: This is the output of `kubectl describe pod` for a pod requesting more memory than any node has free. The `Events:` block is where the scheduler explains its filter phase: read the sentence after `0/3 nodes are available` and count how many nodes each reason removed. Run it as soon as a pod stays Pending for more than a few seconds.

sections.title: Pending pod events
sections.output:
Events:
  Type     Reason            Age   From               Message
  ----     ------            ----  ----               -------
  Warning  FailedScheduling  42s   default-scheduler  0/3 nodes are available: 1 node(s) had untolerated taint {node-role.kubernetes.io/control-plane: }, 2 Insufficient memory. preemption: 0/3 nodes are available: 1 Preemption is not helpful for scheduling, 2 No preemption victims found for incoming pod.
sections.note: Reasons are per node and add up to the node count. Here 1 + 2 = 3 nodes.

sections.title: Requests versus limits
head: Field
Used by
Meaning
Example
rows: Guaranteed share, counted against node allocatable

sections.title: About this example: a pod with explicit requests and limits
sections.body: This is a complete Deployment applied with `kubectl apply -f api.yaml`. Look at the `resources` block: the scheduler only reads `requests` (500m CPU, 512Mi memory per replica, 1.5 cores in total) and ignores `limits`, which are enforced later by the kernel. The gap between request and limit is the burst the container may use if the node has spare capacity.

sections.title: api.yaml
sections.code:
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: api
  namespace: shop
spec:
  replicas: 3
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: api
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: api
    spec:
      containers:
        - name: api
          image: registry.example.com/shop/api:2.4.1
          ports:
            - containerPort: 8080
          resources:
            requests:
              cpu: 500m
              memory: 512Mi
              ephemeral-storage: 1Gi
            limits:
              cpu: "1"
              memory: 768Mi
              ephemeral-storage: 2Gi
sections.note: Scheduling is based on requests only. A node with 8 CPUs idle but 8 CPUs of requests booked is full.

sections.title: About this example: node capacity versus allocatable
sections.body: `kubectl describe node` prints two tables. `Capacity` is the raw hardware, `Allocatable` is what remains for pods after `kube-reserved`, `system-reserved` and the eviction threshold. Below them, `Allocated resources` shows the sum of requests already booked, which is the number the scheduler compares against. Check the percentages in parentheses to find over-booked nodes.

sections.title: Node allocatable and booked requests
sections.output:
Capacity:
  cpu:                4
  ephemeral-storage:  101430960Ki
  memory:             16384000Ki
  pods:               110
Allocatable:
  cpu:                3920m
  ephemeral-storage:  93478772582
  memory:             15281152Ki
  pods:               110
Allocated resources:

exercises.title: Find the over-booked node
exercises.prompt: List allocated CPU and memory requests for every node and find the one closest to 100 percent.
exercises.expected: Each node shows a Requests column with percentages; the busiest node is the most likely to produce Insufficient cpu errors.
exercises.hint: Look at the percentage in parentheses, not the limits column.

exercises.title: Check a pod's QoS class
exercises.prompt: Print the QoS class of one pod and say which resources would need to change to make it Guaranteed.
exercises.command: kubectl get pod api-6d8f7b9c5-4kq2m -n shop -o jsonpath='{.status.qosClass}'
exercises.expected: Burstable, because requests differ from limits.
exercises.hint: Guaranteed needs requests == limits on every container, including sidecars.
exercises.solution: Set cpu and memory requests equal to limits in each container, then recreate the pod.

questions.question: Which resource value does the scheduler use to decide if a pod fits a node?
questions.explain: The scheduler sums requests of pods already on the node and compares against allocatable. Limits and live usage are ignored.

questions.question: A pod has memory requests 256Mi and limits 512Mi. What is its QoS class?
questions.explain: Requests differ from limits, so it is Burstable. Guaranteed needs both to be equal for all containers.

questions.question: What happens when a container exceeds its CPU limit?
questions.explain: CPU is compressible: the CFS quota throttles the container. Only memory overuse leads to a kill.

questions.question: Which pods does the kubelet evict first under memory pressure?
options: BestEffort and Burstable over their request
questions.explain: Eviction ranks by QoS and usage above request, so BestEffort goes first.

sources.title: Resource Management for Pods and Containers

lessons.title: Node selection: affinity, taints and tolerations
lessons.summary: Steer pods with nodeSelector, node and pod affinity, anti-affinity, taints and tolerations.
objectives: Choose between nodeSelector, node affinity and taints for a given requirement
Write required and preferred affinity rules with the right operators
Dedicate nodes to a workload using taint plus toleration plus selector

sections.title: Attract and repel
sections.body:
Placement controls come in two directions. **Attracting** rules live on the pod: `nodeSelector`, `nodeAffinity` (pull to nodes by label) and `podAffinity` / `podAntiAffinity` (pull to or push away from nodes that already run certain pods). **Repelling** rules live on the node: a **taint** keeps every pod away unless it carries a matching **toleration**.

A toleration only *allows* scheduling onto a tainted node, it does not attract. To dedicate a node pool you therefore combine both: taint the nodes so others stay out, and add a selector or affinity so the pods go in.

sections.title: Placement mechanisms compared
head: Mechanism
Defined on
Hard or soft
Typical use
rows: Expressions: In, NotIn, Exists, Gt, Lt

sections.title: About this example: a Deployment with node affinity
sections.body: This Deployment is applied with `kubectl apply -f gpu-infer.yaml`. The `requiredDuringSchedulingIgnoredDuringExecution` block is a hard filter: only nodes labelled `accelerator=nvidia` qualify. The `preferred` block adds up to 80 score points to nodes in the `m5` family without ever excluding others. The `IgnoredDuringExecution` suffix means already-running pods are not moved if labels change later.

sections.title: gpu-infer.yaml
sections.code:
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: gpu-infer
  namespace: ml
spec:
  replicas: 2
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: gpu-infer
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: gpu-infer
    spec:
      affinity:
        nodeAffinity:
          requiredDuringSchedulingIgnoredDuringExecution:
            nodeSelectorTerms:
              - matchExpressions:
                  - key: accelerator
                    operator: In
                    values: ["nvidia"]
          preferredDuringSchedulingIgnoredDuringExecution:
            - weight: 80
              preference:
                matchExpressions:
                  - key: node.kubernetes.io/instance-type
                    operator: In
                    values: ["g5.xlarge", "g5.2xlarge"]
      containers:
        - name: infer
          image: registry.example.com/ml/infer:1.8.0
          resources:
            requests:
              cpu: "2"
              memory: 8Gi
            limits:
              memory: 8Gi
sections.note: nodeSelector is just shorthand for a required In rule with one value. Use affinity when you need OR, NotIn or soft preferences.

sections.title: About this example: taints on nodes
sections.body: Taints are set with `kubectl taint` and read back from the node spec. The format is `key=value:effect`. Look at the three effects: `NoSchedule` blocks new pods, `PreferNoSchedule` is a soft hint, and `NoExecute` also evicts running pods that lack a toleration. Kubernetes itself adds NoExecute taints such as `node.kubernetes.io/unreachable` when a node stops responding.

sections.title: Tainting a dedicated pool
sections.code:
kubectl label node worker-gpu-1 accelerator=nvidia
kubectl taint node worker-gpu-1 dedicated=gpu:NoSchedule
kubectl get node worker-gpu-1 -o jsonpath='{.spec.taints}'
kubectl taint node worker-gpu-1 dedicated=gpu:NoSchedule-
sections.output:
node/worker-gpu-1 labeled
node/worker-gpu-1 tainted
[{"effect":"NoSchedule","key":"dedicated","value":"gpu"}]
node/worker-gpu-1 untainted
sections.note: A trailing minus removes a taint or label. Existing pods stay when you add NoSchedule; use NoExecute to push them out.

sections.title: About this example: pod with toleration and pod anti-affinity
sections.body: This Deployment tolerates the `dedicated=gpu` taint and also uses `podAntiAffinity` with the key `kubernetes.io/hostname`, which means no two `web` replicas may share a node. The `topologyKey` defines what counts as the same place: hostname means one node, a zone label means one zone. Also note the `tolerationSeconds: 60` for `not-ready`, which shortens the default 300 seconds before eviction.

sections.title: web-spread.yaml
sections.code:
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: web
  namespace: shop
spec:
  replicas: 3
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: web
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: web
    spec:
      tolerations:
        - key: dedicated
          operator: Equal
          value: gpu
          effect: NoSchedule
        - key: node.kubernetes.io/not-ready
          operator: Exists
          effect: NoExecute
          tolerationSeconds: 60
      affinity:
        podAntiAffinity:
          requiredDuringSchedulingIgnoredDuringExecution:
            - labelSelector:
                matchLabels:
                  app: web
              topologyKey: kubernetes.io/hostname
      containers:
        - name: web
          image: nginx:1.27-alpine
          resources:
            requests:
              cpu: 100m
              memory: 128Mi
sections.note: Required anti-affinity with more replicas than nodes leaves extra pods Pending. Use preferred, or topology spread constraints, when that is not acceptable.

exercises.prompt: Taint a node with env=batch:NoSchedule and show that the taint is present.
exercises.hint: Check with kubectl describe node worker-2 | grep Taints.
exercises.solution: kubectl taint node worker-2 env=batch:NoSchedule-   # remove again when done

exercises.title: Why Pending?
exercises.prompt: A pod is Pending. Print only the scheduling failure message.
exercises.expected: One FailedScheduling line per blocked pod with per-node reasons.

questions.question: What does a toleration do?
options: Attracts a pod to tainted nodes
Allows a pod to be scheduled on a tainted node
questions.explain: A toleration only permits placement; it does not attract.

questions.question: Which taint effect also evicts already-running pods?
questions.explain: NoExecute removes running pods that do not tolerate the taint.

questions.question: What does topologyKey kubernetes.io/hostname mean in a podAntiAffinity rule?
options: Pods may not share the same node
questions.explain: The topologyKey defines the domain; hostname makes each node its own domain.

questions.question: Why is IgnoredDuringExecution in the field name important?
options: Pods are evicted when labels change
Rules are checked only at scheduling time
questions.explain: Running pods are not moved if node labels change after scheduling.

lessons.title: Topology spread and zone-aware HA
lessons.summary: Use topologySpreadConstraints to spread replicas across zones and nodes and survive a zone outage.
objectives: Write a topologySpreadConstraint with maxSkew, topologyKey and whenUnsatisfiable
Compute skew for a given pod distribution
Combine zone and node spreading and handle rolling updates

sections.title: Why spread beyond anti-affinity
sections.body:
Required pod anti-affinity gives a binary rule: one replica per node, and extra replicas stay Pending. **Topology spread constraints** express *evenness*: replicas should be balanced across failure domains such as zones and nodes, within a tolerated imbalance called `maxSkew`.

**Skew** for a domain is the number of matching pods in it minus the minimum count in any eligible domain. With 2, 2 and 1 pods in three zones the skew is 1. With `maxSkew: 1` the next pod must go to the zone holding 1, otherwise it would raise skew to 2.

sections.title: Fields of topologySpreadConstraints
head: Field
Meaning
Typical value
Effect
rows: What to do if skew would be exceeded
Must match the pod's own labels
Counts empty domains so new zones get pods
Extra label keys to scope counting

sections.title: About this example: a zone and node spread Deployment
sections.body: This Deployment is applied with `kubectl apply -f web-ha.yaml`. The first constraint is hard (`DoNotSchedule`) across zones with `maxSkew: 1`, so a six-replica Deployment on three zones lands 2/2/2. The second constraint is soft across nodes, so the scheduler tries to avoid stacking but never leaves a pod Pending because of it. `matchLabelKeys: [pod-template-hash]` keeps rolling updates balanced per ReplicaSet.

sections.title: web-ha.yaml
sections.code:
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: web-ha
  namespace: shop
spec:
  replicas: 6
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: web-ha
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: web-ha
    spec:
      topologySpreadConstraints:
        - maxSkew: 1
          topologyKey: topology.kubernetes.io/zone
          whenUnsatisfiable: DoNotSchedule
          labelSelector:
            matchLabels:
              app: web-ha
          matchLabelKeys:
            - pod-template-hash
        - maxSkew: 1
          topologyKey: kubernetes.io/hostname
          whenUnsatisfiable: ScheduleAnyway
          labelSelector:
            matchLabels:
              app: web-ha
      containers:
        - name: web
          image: nginx:1.27-alpine
          resources:
            requests:
              cpu: 200m
              memory: 256Mi
sections.note: The labelSelector must match the pod template labels, otherwise the constraint counts nothing.

sections.title: About this example: checking the zone distribution
sections.body: Zone labels are set by the cloud provider, and you can show them as a column. Then group pods by node and map nodes to zones to confirm the 2/2/2 spread. Use this check after every scaling event or node pool change.

sections.title: About this example: cluster-wide defaults
sections.body: Instead of repeating constraints in every manifest, the scheduler can apply default spreading to pods that define none. This file is a fragment of a `KubeSchedulerConfiguration` passed to `kube-scheduler --config` on self-managed clusters; managed services usually spread by zone by default already. Look at `defaultingType: List`, which replaces the built-in defaults with your own list.

sections.title: scheduler-config.yaml fragment
sections.code:
apiVersion: kubescheduler.config.k8s.io/v1
kind: KubeSchedulerConfiguration
profiles:
  - schedulerName: default-scheduler
    pluginConfig:
      - name: PodTopologySpread
        args:
          defaultingType: List
          defaultConstraints:
            - maxSkew: 1
              topologyKey: topology.kubernetes.io/zone
              whenUnsatisfiable: ScheduleAnyway
sections.note: The built-in default (defaultingType System) already spreads by hostname and zone softly.

questions.explain: Zone a would raise skew to 2; b or c keep it at 1.

questions.question: Which whenUnsatisfiable value never leaves a pod Pending because of the constraint?
questions.explain: ScheduleAnyway only influences scoring.

questions.question: What does skew measure?
options: Difference between the fullest and emptiest domain

questions.question: Why use matchLabelKeys with pod-template-hash?

modules.title: Priority, disruption and capacity
modules.summary: Who wins under pressure, how to stay available and how to scale.

lessons.title: Priority, preemption and PodDisruptionBudgets
lessons.summary: Rank workloads with PriorityClass, understand preemption, and protect availability with PDBs.
objectives: Create PriorityClasses and assign them to pods
Explain how preemption chooses victims and its limits
Write a PodDisruptionBudget and predict how it affects drains

sections.title: Who wins when the cluster is full
sections.body:
A **PriorityClass** gives pods an integer rank. When a high-priority pod is Pending because no node fits, the scheduler's **PostFilter** step may **preempt**: it finds a node where evicting lower-priority pods would let the pod fit, deletes those victims (respecting their graceful termination), and nominates the node for the pending pod via `status.nominatedNodeName`.

Priority is not QoS. Priority decides who may displace whom at **scheduling** time and ordering in the queue. QoS decides who the kubelet kills first under **node pressure**. A PodDisruptionBudget sits on yet another axis: it limits **voluntary** disruptions such as drains and the eviction API. Preemption honours PDBs only on a best-effort basis.

sections.title: About this example: PriorityClasses
sections.body: These two objects are applied with `kubectl apply -f priorities.yaml`. `business-critical` has a high value and may preempt; `batch-low` uses `preemptionPolicy: Never`, meaning its pods queue ahead of lower ones but never evict anyone. `globalDefault: true` would assign a class to every pod without one, so only one class may carry it. Values above 1 billion are reserved for `system-cluster-critical` and `system-node-critical`.

sections.title: priorities.yaml
sections.code:
apiVersion: scheduling.k8s.io/v1
kind: PriorityClass
metadata:
  name: business-critical
value: 100000
globalDefault: false
preemptionPolicy: PreemptLowerPriority
description: Customer-facing services that may displace batch work.
---
apiVersion: scheduling.k8s.io/v1
kind: PriorityClass
metadata:
  name: batch-low
value: 1000
globalDefault: false
preemptionPolicy: Never
description: Batch jobs that wait rather than evict others.

sections.title: About this example: a PodDisruptionBudget
sections.body: This PDB is applied with `kubectl apply -f checkout-pdb.yaml`. It says at least 2 `checkout` pods must stay available during voluntary disruptions. Use either `minAvailable` or `maxUnavailable`, never both; percentages are allowed. `unhealthyPodEvictionPolicy: AlwaysAllow` lets the drain evict pods that are already not Ready, so a crashlooping pod cannot block node maintenance.

sections.title: checkout-pdb.yaml
sections.code:
apiVersion: policy/v1
kind: PodDisruptionBudget
metadata:
  name: checkout-pdb
  namespace: shop
spec:
  minAvailable: 2
  unhealthyPodEvictionPolicy: AlwaysAllow
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: checkout

sections.title: About this example: the PDB in action during a drain
sections.body: `kubectl get pdb` shows `ALLOWED DISRUPTIONS`, the number of pods that can be evicted right now (healthy pods minus minAvailable). When a drain would drop below the budget the eviction API answers 429 and `kubectl drain` retries every five seconds until pods are rescheduled elsewhere. Read the repeated error line as normal waiting, not as a failure.

sections.title: Drain respecting a PDB
sections.code:
kubectl get pdb -n shop
kubectl drain worker-1 --ignore-daemonsets --delete-emptydir-data
sections.output:
NAME           MIN AVAILABLE   MAX UNAVAILABLE   ALLOWED DISRUPTIONS   AGE
checkout-pdb   2               N/A               1                     6m

node/worker-1 cordoned
evicting pod shop/checkout-6c5b7d8f9-4lq2w
error when evicting pods/"checkout-6c5b7d8f9-9mtzs" -n "shop" (will retry after 5s): Cannot evict pod as it would violate the pod's disruption budget.
pod/checkout-6c5b7d8f9-4lq2w evicted
node/worker-1 drained
sections.note: Three replicas with minAvailable 2 allow one eviction at a time.

sections.title: The two classic PDB mistakes
sections.body: A PDB with `minAvailable` equal to the replica count (or a single-replica Deployment with `minAvailable: 1`) allows **zero** disruptions and stalls node upgrades and the cluster autoscaler. The opposite mistake is having no PDB at all, so a drain evicts every replica at once. Also remember a PDB does not protect against node crashes or preemption guarantees: preemption tries to respect PDBs but may violate them if no other victims exist.

exercises.title: Inspect the budget
exercises.prompt: Show the PDB and how many pods can currently be disrupted.
exercises.expected: ALLOWED DISRUPTIONS column shows an integer.
exercises.hint: Describe the PDB to see current/desired healthy counts.

exercises.title: List priorities used
exercises.prompt: Show the priority class and value for every pod in a namespace.
exercises.expected: A table with class name and numeric priority.
exercises.solution: Pods with no class show <none> and priority 0.

questions.question: What does preemptionPolicy: Never mean?
options: Pods of this class are never scheduled
The pod is queued by priority but never evicts others
questions.explain: Never keeps queue ordering but disables evicting lower-priority pods.

questions.question: A PDB applies to which kind of disruption?
questions.explain: PDBs guard voluntary disruptions through the Eviction API.

questions.question: Three replicas and minAvailable: 3. What happens during kubectl drain?
options: It blocks because zero disruptions are allowed
questions.explain: No pod may be evicted, so the drain keeps retrying.

questions.question: Which setting can lead to PDB deadlock with crashlooping pods?
questions.explain: By default unhealthy pods count against the budget and may block eviction; AlwaysAllow avoids that.

lessons.title: Cluster autoscaler, VPA, KEDA and capacity planning
lessons.summary: Scale nodes and pods with Cluster Autoscaler, VPA and KEDA, and plan headroom with real numbers.
objectives: Explain how Cluster Autoscaler reacts to Pending pods and idle nodes
Use VPA recommendations to right-size requests
Describe event-driven scaling with KEDA and size cluster headroom

sections.title: Three scaling axes
sections.body:
**Horizontal Pod Autoscaler** changes replica count from metrics. **Vertical Pod Autoscaler (VPA)** changes the CPU and memory *requests* of each pod. **Cluster Autoscaler (CA)** or Karpenter changes the number of *nodes*. They chain: HPA adds pods, pods go Pending, CA sees Pending pods that would fit on a new node and adds one. When nodes sit under about 50 percent utilisation of requests for ten minutes and their pods can move, CA removes them.

CA reasons purely from requests and scheduling constraints. That is why accurate requests (lesson 1) and honest PDBs (lesson 4) decide whether autoscaling is smooth or stuck.

sections.title: About this example: Cluster Autoscaler in action
sections.body: These are events and the CA status ConfigMap on a cluster where a burst of pods went Pending. The `TriggeredScaleUp` event shows the node group growing from 3 to 5, and the status block lists health per group. Use this to confirm the autoscaler sees the pods; if `NotTriggerScaleUp` appears, its message tells you the constraint (max size reached, no group has the right taint or label).

sections.title: Cluster Autoscaler events
sections.code:
kubectl get events -A --field-selector reason=TriggeredScaleUp
kubectl -n kube-system get configmap cluster-autoscaler-status -o jsonpath='{.data.status}' | head -12
sections.output:
NAMESPACE   LAST SEEN   TYPE     REASON             OBJECT                  MESSAGE
shop        90s         Normal   TriggeredScaleUp   pod/web-ha-6b8d9f7c4-p5mzs   pod triggered scale-up: [{eks-workers-a 3->5 (max: 8)}]

sections.title: About this example: a VerticalPodAutoscaler in recommendation mode
sections.body: This VPA is applied with `kubectl apply -f api-vpa.yaml` and requires the VPA components installed. `updateMode: "Off"` makes it only compute recommendations without restarting pods, the safest way to start. `controlledValues: RequestsOnly` leaves limits alone, and `minAllowed` / `maxAllowed` bound the suggestions.

sections.title: api-vpa.yaml
sections.code:
apiVersion: autoscaling.k8s.io/v1
kind: VerticalPodAutoscaler
metadata:
  name: api-vpa
  namespace: shop
spec:
  targetRef:
    apiVersion: apps/v1
    kind: Deployment
    name: api
  updatePolicy:
    updateMode: "Off"
  resourcePolicy:
    containerPolicies:
      - containerName: api
        controlledValues: RequestsOnly
        minAllowed:
          cpu: 100m
          memory: 128Mi
        maxAllowed:
          cpu: "2"
          memory: 2Gi

sections.title: About this example: reading VPA recommendations
sections.body: After the VPA has watched the pods for a while, `describe` prints a Recommendation block. `Lower Bound` is the minimum safe request, `Target` is what the VPA would set, and `Upper Bound` is the ceiling accounting for uncertainty. Here the Deployment requests 500m / 512Mi but the target is 180m / 310Mi, so you are paying for about 64 percent idle CPU request.

sections.title: VPA recommendation output
sections.code: kubectl describe vpa api-vpa -n shop | sed -n '/Recommendation:/,$p'
sections.output:
Recommendation:
    Container Recommendations:
      Container Name:  api
      Lower Bound:
        Cpu:     120m
        Memory:  256Mi
      Target:
        Cpu:     180m
        Memory:  310Mi
      Uncapped Target:
        Cpu:     180m
        Memory:  310Mi
      Upper Bound:
        Cpu:     420m
        Memory:  520Mi
sections.note: Copy Target values into your manifests during a review instead of enabling Auto mode in production.

sections.title: About this example: KEDA ScaledObject
sections.body: KEDA (a CNCF project) scales a Deployment from external signals, including down to zero. This `ScaledObject` is applied with `kubectl apply -f worker-keda.yaml` once KEDA is installed. The `trigger` of type `rabbitmq` scales so that each replica handles about 20 queued messages, between 0 and 30 replicas, and `cooldownPeriod` waits 5 minutes before returning to zero. The connection string comes from a TriggerAuthentication, never inline.

sections.title: worker-keda.yaml
sections.code:
apiVersion: keda.sh/v1alpha1
kind: ScaledObject
metadata:
  name: order-worker
  namespace: shop
spec:
  scaleTargetRef:
    name: order-worker
  minReplicaCount: 0
  maxReplicaCount: 30
  cooldownPeriod: 300
  triggers:
    - type: rabbitmq
      metadata:
        queueName: orders
        mode: QueueLength
        value: "20"
      authenticationRef:
        name: rabbitmq-auth

exercises.title: Spot scale-up evidence
exercises.prompt: Find evidence that Cluster Autoscaler added nodes recently.
exercises.expected: One event per scale-up with group sizes.
exercises.hint: If empty, no scale-up happened or it is not installed.

exercises.title: Compare request to recommendation
exercises.prompt: Read the VPA recommendation for the api Deployment and compare it with its current request.
exercises.expected: Target CPU/memory differ from the current requests.

questions.question: What causes Cluster Autoscaler to add a node?
options: High CPU usage on a node
Pending pods that would fit on a new node
questions.explain: CA reacts to unschedulable pods, not to live CPU load.

questions.question: Which VPA updateMode only computes recommendations?
questions.explain: Off produces recommendations without touching pods.

questions.question: What can KEDA do that plain HPA cannot do out of the box?
options: Scale to zero from external event sources
questions.explain: KEDA supports many external scalers and scaling workloads to and from zero.

questions.question: Why keep overprovisioning pause pods at a low priority?
options: Real pods preempt them to start instantly while new nodes join
questions.explain: Preemption frees ready-made space immediately, hiding node start-up time.
